name: Calcium hydroxide relaxer

lead: A calcium hydroxide relaxer is the 'no-lye' alternative to the traditional sodium hydroxide cream, used to straighten tightly curled hair. It is mixed with a guanidine activator before use.
It is often marketed toward people with sensitive scalps.

paras: Calcium hydroxide and guanidine carbonate react to form guanidine hydroxide, a weaker alkali that breaks the hair's disulfide bonds.
Burns, dermatitis and breakage are reported for both lye and no-lye relaxers. Observational health studies have not separated product types, and cosmetics are not pre-approved by the FDA.

lead: A calcium hydroxide relaxer, marketed as a 'no-lye' relaxer, is a chemical hair straightener in which calcium hydroxide (slaked lime) is mixed at the time of use with an activating solution of guanidine carbonate, producing guanidine hydroxide as the active agent.[1] Guanidine hydroxide is described as a weaker alkaline agent than sodium hydroxide, and these products are positioned as an option for sensitive scalps.[1][2]

Like all relaxers, it permanently alters treated hair by breaking disulfide bonds, and new growth is unaffected.[2] Wikipedia notes that both lye and no-lye relaxers can cause severe chemical burns and breakage, and that available health studies do not separate calcium-based products from sodium hydroxide ones.[1]
infobox: Guanidine hydroxide, from calcium hydroxide plus guanidine carbonate[1]

paras: Calcium hydroxide and a guanidine carbonate activating solution are combined shortly before use, generating guanidine hydroxide.[1] The resulting alkali breaks the disulfide bonds of the hair shaft in a similar way to lye products, though it is regarded as milder.[1][2]

Wikipedia reports the first commercial no-lye product, using potassium hydroxide, appeared in 1919.[1] In the 1990s the Rio Hair Naturalizer System, marketed as chemical-free, was associated with scalp damage and hair loss, led to a class action and was withdrawn.[1]

Both lye and no-lye relaxers can cause scalp burns, irritant or allergic dermatitis, brittleness and breakage, with severe chemical burns possible after overexposure.[1] The article gives no separate risk profile for calcium hydroxide products.[1]

No studies specific to calcium hydroxide relaxers were identified. Studies of relaxer use generally, including associations with uterine fibroids and with breast and uterine cancer, did not analyse products by alkali type, so they provide no comparison of the two types.[1]

timeline.event: First commercial no-lye product (potassium hydroxide) reported.[1]
